title: CJI to Decide Fate of Plea to Recall Split Verdict on Election Commission Law
excerpt: A curative plea argues Justice Satish Chandra Sharma’s undisclosed family link to the Election Commission vitiates the September 23 split verdict on the CEC appointment law — and only the Chief Justice can decide what happens next.
body:
• The Chief Justice of India will take a call on how the Supreme Court handles a curative plea seeking recall of part of its September 23 split verdict on the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
  • The plea, filed by Dr Jaya Thakur and Naman Sherstra, argues Justice Satish Chandra Sharma never disclosed that his son, Siddharth Sharma, has been standing counsel for the Election Commission before the Madhya Pradesh High Court since July 10, 2024 — creating a "reasonable apprehension of bias."
  • Justice Dipankar Datta, who sat on the split bench, declined to hear the recall application himself and directed that it be mentioned before the Chief Justice.
  • What changes for now: nothing. The 2023 law stays in force and appointments already made under it are untouched until the reference question — and now the recall plea — is decided.

The Chief Justice of India will decide how the Supreme Court handles a plea seeking recall of one half of its September 23 split verdict on the law governing appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners. The application was mentioned before Justice Dipankar Datta, the senior judge on the bench that delivered the split ruling, who directed that it be placed before the Chief Justice — the ordinary route for a matter already in the CJI's office.

The recall plea and the undisclosed link

The curative petition, filed by Dr Jaya Thakur and Naman Sherstra, invokes "reasonable apprehension of bias and propriety." It contends that Justice Satish Chandra Sharma — the second judge on the bench that delivered the September 23 verdict — neither disclosed that his son is standing counsel for the Election Commission nor recused himself.

https://x.com/PTI_News/status/2107722134906966156

According to the applicants, the bench heard the matter on five occasions. They say they learned of the connection only after the verdict, from press reports, and then verified it from the Madhya Pradesh High Court website: Siddharth Sharma has been empanelled with the Election Commission since July 10, 2024. The plea argues Justice Sharma's presence on the bench vitiated the decision under the Supreme Court's "reasonable likelihood of bias" and "real danger" tests.

The applicants seek recall of Justice Sharma's opinion and a fresh hearing — but do not ask for Justice Datta's separate opinion to be wiped out. Justice Datta declined to deal with the application himself. Since the September 23 order is already with the Chief Justice for constitution of a larger bench, a plea alleging that one half of the split is vitiated has to be listed by the same office.

What the September 23 split was actually about

The split verdict did not decide whether the 2023 Act is valid. It split on a prior question: should that challenge go to a Constitution Bench? Justice Datta held no reference was required, and recorded prima facie doubts about the selection panel created by the law — in which a Union cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister replaced the Chief Justice of India.

"A Minister could not be expected to defy the Prime Minister."

— Justice Dipankar Datta, in his September 23 opinion on the election-chief selection panel

Justice Datta held that the arrangement failed the "perception test" and that the Leader of the Opposition's role on the panel was largely ornamental. Justice Sharma disagreed, holding that a substantial question of constitutional interpretation was involved and favouring a bench of at least five judges under Article 145(3). Both judges directed that the papers be placed before the Chief Justice.

Why the stakes run high

The immediate practical effect of the recall plea is delay. The 2023 law remains in force, and a final word on whether Parliament could remove the Chief Justice from the panel — handing the executive a standing majority of two against the Leader of the Opposition — is now further off.

The bias application also lands in a week of parallel scrutiny of the poll panel. On October 5, a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant refused to suspend CEC Gyanesh Kumar over allegations that he took decisions unilaterally during the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls, without the consensus of the two other Election Commissioners. Issuing notices to the Centre and the Election Commission to respond within a week, the court warned that if any decisions were found to have been taken without unanimity, it would "take those decisions back."

What's next

The Chief Justice now has two options on the recall plea: list the bias application before a different bench, or fold it into the larger-bench exercise and have the reference question heard afresh. A recall is not the likely end — the court rarely erases a reasoned opinion on a non-disclosure allegation, particularly where the son's retainer is before another court.

Either course keeps the validity of the 2023 Act undecided for months. The plea tests judicial disclosure norms first; the statute itself waits behind it.
